title: Seven ninths or seventeen twenty-firsts: which is greater?
description: Seven ninths and seventeen twenty-firsts are compared by finding a common multiple of nine and twenty-one. Counting in the bigger bottom number shows sixty-three, a smaller common unit than the product. Keeko doubts the answer by saying ninths are bigger pieces, so seven ninths wins.
teaching_notes: One idea: count in the bigger bottom number until the smaller one fits, then compare the top numbers. Watch for students who compare the size of one piece and forget the number of pieces.

video_script.why: A learner finds a small common multiple by counting in the bigger bottom number, then compares the top numbers.
video_script.substitution: the book's own pair seven ninths and seventeen twenty-firsts
video_script.anchor: the pair seven ninths and seventeen twenty-firsts as two bars of the same length
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says seven ninths is greater because ninths are bigger pieces than twenty-firsts, and forgets that the other fraction has seventeen pieces.
video_script.payoff_line: seventeen twenty-firsts is greater than seven ninths

final_answer.spoken: seven ninths is forty-nine sixty-thirds and seventeen twenty-firsts is fifty-one sixty-thirds, so seventeen twenty-firsts is greater than seven ninths

video_script.fraction_reading: seven ninths, seventeen twenty-firsts, forty-nine sixty-thirds, fifty-one sixty-thirds
never_show: a tick on 7/9 before the working
maths_rules: multiples of 21: 21, 42, 63; 9 x 7 = 63, so 63 is a common multiple of 9 and 21
slip: Keeko says 7/9 is greater because ninths are bigger pieces than twenty-firsts; but 17 pieces of 1/21 make 51/63 and 7 pieces of 1/9 make 49/63
video_script.design: Two bars of the same length, one cut in ninths and one cut in twenty-firsts. Counting in twenty-ones finds sixty-three without the large product, and the top numbers forty-nine and fifty-one are compared.

narration: <bookmark mark='units'/>Ninths and twenty-firsts are pieces of different sizes, so we need a common multiple of nine and twenty-one.

beats.on_screen: To find: which fraction is greater
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which of the two fractions is greater.

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step one, count in the bigger bottom number. Twenty-one, forty-two, sixty-three.
<bookmark mark='fit'/>Nine times seven is sixty-three, so sixty-three is a common multiple of nine and twenty-one.

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step two, multiply the top and the bottom of seven ninths by seven.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Seven times seven over nine times seven is forty-nine sixty-thirds.

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step three, multiply the top and the bottom of seventeen twenty-firsts by three.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Seventeen times three over twenty-one times three is fifty-one sixty-thirds.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: both in sixty-thirds; compare the numbers of sixty-thirds: 49 and 51

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step four, both fractions are counted in the same unit, so we compare the top numbers. One has forty-nine, and the other has fifty-one.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Forty-nine is less than fifty-one, so seventeen twenty-firsts is greater than seven ninths.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks seven ninths is greater, because ninths are bigger pieces than twenty-firsts.
<bookmark mark='count'/>The pieces are bigger, but the other fraction has seventeen pieces, not seven.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The size of a piece and the number of pieces both matter, so we need one unit.
